location: The 2009 baseline and cross-report comparison.
why: The claim mixes estimates produced under different race/Hispanic-origin adjustments. Using the revised 2009 count of 159,800 gives growth to 160,100 of approximately 0.2%, not 36%.

location: Comparing the 2009 and 2021 estimates across the methodology change.
why: The endpoints use different methods for assigning Hispanic origin. Revising the same 2018 population reduced its estimated count by about 28%, so the reported 26% decline cannot establish a real decline or its ranking against other groups.

location: The parser's dictionary keys and the interpretation of the resulting encounters series.
why: Repeated headers overwrite earlier blocks, leaving Field Operations encounters rather than total encounters. Those port encounters include programme participants, so their increase cannot establish that illegal crossings increased or that legal entry failed to substitute for them.

location: series[col.header] = col.values inside the block loop.
why: Repeated headers overwrite earlier blocks, leaving Border Patrol data labeled as total encounters. The −91% estimate therefore excludes port encounters, whose increase matters for the claimed total-workload effect.

location: Identifying fault-attributed crash damage with the with-against-without effect of the group's driving.
why: Harm in crashes assigned to a group's drivers is not the same as the change in other residents' total crash harm when that driving is removed. The traffic-volume evidence makes that distinction consequential, and subtracting liability payments does not supply the missing counterfactual.

location: Equating fault-assigned crash damages with the with-against-without effect.
why: Removing the group’s driving also changes other drivers’ crash risk, including crashes involving no group driver. The positive traffic-volume elasticity supplies evidence of this omitted effect, so fault-assigned damages net of insurance do not identify the claimed counterfactual cost.

location: acs_cells.py panel filter and attribution of its totals
why: The filter includes imputed-unauthorized workers of every origin, so the resulting $6.43bn and $4.53bn cannot be attributed entirely to the Mexican-origin population. The calculation needs a Mexican-origin restriction and recomputation using the industry-specific rates; the approximate Mexico-born wage share is not an exact correction.

location: acs_cells.py`: the `panel` filter lacks a Mexican-origin restriction.
why: The calculation includes imputed unauthorized wage earners of every origin, then credits their entire withholding to the Mexican-origin population. Mexico-born workers earning about half of those wages demonstrates the material population mismatch, although the exact correction requires identifying Mexican origin.

location: Adding murder costs to assault and robbery costs that already include resulting deaths.
why: This counts homicide losses twice. Removing just the identified overlapping components subtracts $314 per adult-year, reducing the total to $1,107 and raising murder’s share to approximately 83.5%, rather than 65%.

location: Adding $890 of Medicaid savings to the $1,420 care valuation
why: Avoided institutional-care costs already constitute 61% of the care valuation, approximately $866. Adding the nursing-home savings separately double-counts an overlapping benefit and overstates the total.

location: Equating uncharged spending with instructional resources forgone by incumbent pupils.
why: Spending elasticity below one can reflect spare capacity or fixed costs, without reducing instructional quality. Multiplying the accounting residual by an instructional share and intervention effect estimates does not establish the claimed dilution or earnings loss.

location: “full per-pupil funding cannot coexist with diluted instruction”
why: Constant spending per pupil does not guarantee constant instructional provision when pupils have different resource needs. The evidence does not establish that targeted funding fully covers those needs or excludes transition costs during the two-year adjustment, so zero dilution does not follow.

location: Cross-census nativity classification underlying the custody ratios
why: The 2000 allocation procedure assigns almost all missing birthplaces to the US, potentially removing foreign-born institutionalized men from the immigrant numerator and adding them to the native comparator. Earlier censuses handle missing birthplace differently, so these ratios cannot establish improving cohort selection without addressing the measurement break.

location: Comparing custody ratios across the round-3 change in birthplace allocation.
why: Round 3 assigns foreign birth disproportionately to institutionalized cases with missing birthplace, using household donors, whereas earlier rounds dropped missing cases. This measurement change can generate an apparent increase without worsening arrival-cohort selection; the small round-1-to-round-2 difference also does not establish a trend.

location: Inferring unbiased imputed incomes from equal nonresponse rates
why: Equal missingness rates do not establish that donor incomes appropriately represent each group. Income matching omits Hispanic origin, and the supplied comparisons show substantial attenuation of the group’s wage gap, undermining the claim that including imputations leaves its taxable income unbiased.

location: The inference from equal supplement nonresponse rates to unbiased benefit imputation.
why: Equal nonresponse rates do not ensure that donors represent either group’s missing benefit answers. The fill-ins substantially erase the observed within-cell receipt gap, so using their amounts can inflate the group’s benefit allocation; the evidence does not establish absence of bias.

location: The comparison of returnees with people who never migrated.
why: Whether return migration raises US stayers’ average schooling depends on returnees’ schooling relative to migrants remaining in the US. Lower schooling than nonmigrants in Mexico does not establish that relationship, and the survey omits the necessary comparison group.

location: The comparison group used to infer return-migration selection
why: Returnees are compared with never-migrants in Mexico, whereas the claim requires comparison with migrants remaining in the US. Returnees could exceed never-migrants' schooling while having less schooling than US stayers, in which case their departure raises stayers' average.

location: Treating 24,000 flags as a national upper bound and excluding every contest.
why: Incomplete audits with unmeasured missed cases cannot supply an upper bound, even when many flags are false positives. A national aggregate also cannot rule out effects in individual contests decided by 187 or 6 votes without geographically specific evidence.

location: Treating audit flags as confirmed ballots and comparing national flags with a district’s winning margin.
why: Flags include citizens and do not establish that anyone cast a ballot, so 24,000 is not a demonstrated lower bound on noncitizen votes. Even confirmed national votes would not establish enough votes favoring the winner in any particular district to change its outcome.

location: founder_profile`: status-independent treatment at ages 65+.
why: The model omits retirement and healthcare eligibility differences that legalization can create, mechanically suppressing its estimated fiscal effect. The senior-cost sensitivity shows this omission could matter substantially; the 1.9% result does not establish that legal status hardly matters.

location: founder_profile(), where legalization changes benefits but leaves earnings and taxes fixed.
why: The model omits documented earnings and payroll-reporting responses that would affect tax receipts and potentially benefit amounts. The 34% result therefore describes this restricted benefits-change scenario rather than establishing legalization's overall fiscal effect.

location: Inference from all-household SSI receipt to native households' receipt.
why: Because immigrant households have lower SSI receipt, increasing their share can lower the aggregate rate even if native receipt stays constant or rises. The strong first stage does not resolve this composition problem.

location: The inference about natives from an all-household outcome.
why: The aggregate outcome cannot distinguish changes in natives' receipt from changes in household composition. At the supplied rates, a one-percentage-point increase in immigrant household share mechanically raises aggregate receipt by 0.027 percentage points with both groups' rates unchanged, nearly the reported effect. A strong first stage does not resolve this outcome mismatch.

location: “Did not lose ground” and “none of those mechanisms moves with the shares.”
why: The immigrant-origin estimate has an approximate 95% interval of −0.070 to +0.032 SD, allowing meaningful losses; statistical nonsignificance does not establish their absence. Likewise, cut-score intervals permitting declines of 7–13 points do not establish that standards are unrelated to the shares.

location: none
why: The claim describes a negative association supported by the reported estimates and robustness checks, and explicitly conditions the earnings interpretation on causality. Remaining confounding limits a causal conclusion but does not contradict the stated association.

location: none
why: The evidence supports a national-bin discrepancy and a conditional recalculation that preserves the group's within-bin shares. Pooling and the alternative cutoff address the stated sparse-tail sensitivity; the recalculation does not independently validate the group's actual tax liability.

location: none

Alternative pooling gives a similar result; this supports the candidate correction without independently validating the group’s within-bin shares.

location: none

Repairing that mismatch is justified; the post hoc comparison and weak identification leave the key uncertain without establishing that it needs correction.

location: none
why: The prespecified comparison provides limited support for uninsured exposure over population weighting. It does not establish superiority over a simple uninsured count or validate the group's particular allocation, and the insured costs in S-10 limit comparability; those limits do not overturn the modest claim of support.

location: none
why: The population key has the smaller distance on the prespecified state-share comparison, supporting its stated status as a candidate. Insured patients in S-10 and the confounded slope limit conclusions about uninsured or Mexican-origin use; the different national totals do not invalidate a comparison of normalized state shares.

location: none
why: An annual accrual can recognize the present value of future losses caused by that year's exposure. Booking each exposure's incremental harm once, separating accruals from cash flows, and excluding duplicate tax losses avoids the stated stock/flow and double-counting errors.

location: none
why: An annual accrual can recognize the present value of future benefits caused by that year's exposure. The stated accounting assigns each incremental benefit once and avoids separately adding taxes already included in gross earnings.

location: none
why: The specified victim costs exclude police, adjudication and corrections, so adding them to those fiscal spending lines does not duplicate those costs. The separate homicide treatment also removes the stated source of overlapping death valuation.

location: Adding consumer savings “to its fiscal receipts line”
why: The exclusions can make consumer savings a distinct welfare benefit, but they do not make it government revenue. The $9.4bn belongs in a broader welfare balance; adding it to fiscal receipts would understate the fiscal cost.

location: none
why: The reported winner shares and the maximum across existing scenarios are all below 50%. Allocation sensitivity limits generalization, but the claim explicitly conditions its conclusion on those allocations; nearly cancelling dollar totals do not imply equal numbers of winners and losers.

location: none
why: Every reported scenario, including the enumerated minimum, has a majority of winners. Allocation sensitivity limits generalization, but the claim explicitly confines its conclusion to these incidence scenarios.

location: “reflects the census’s birthplace allocation, not selection” and “the same men reappear”
why: The allocation sensitivity demonstrates a potentially substantial measurement distortion but does not isolate allocation from selection. Repeated census and ACS cross-sections do not track the same individuals, and changing age, residence duration and period can also change custody rates; the weaker conclusion that progressively stronger selection is not demonstrated remains defensible.

location: Attributing the spike definitively to allocation and dismissing successive-cohort deterioration.
why: Redistributing allocated birthplaces in respondents’ proportions assumes that respondents represent those with missing birthplace; the sensitivity calculation does not establish that assumption. A later survey does not track the same individual men, and the matched-duration ratios actually increase across successive cohorts, 0.53→0.58→0.61, although their statistical significance is unknown.

location: none
why: The comparable estimators produce closely matching gaps, and the reported ratios are correct. This supports replication across survey instruments, with the explicit limitation that neither survey validates earnings against tax records.

location: none
why: The ratios correctly describe close agreement between estimates using the same target population and standardization. This supports replication across surveys, with the explicitly acknowledged limitation that neither survey validates the estimates against tax records.

location: none
why: Fault attribution and the change in other residents’ crash costs under traffic removal measure different things. Conditional on the stated transferability assumptions, near-zero risk elasticities support a smaller incremental burden, while the reported range explicitly leaves its magnitude and sign uncertain.

location: none
why: A with-versus-without calculation can include additional crashes among other residents that fault attribution omits. The stated elasticity sensitivity reproduces the dollar range: ±0.42 implies approximately ±$22.7bn around $72.1bn. No conclusion-changing error is demonstrated, although the studies' transferability cannot be independently established from this excerpt.

location: none
why: The working-age ratio directly compares the group's observed spending with the spending assigned by its own cells' donor means, supporting overprediction on this survey file. The claim appropriately declines to infer a difference at 65+, where the interval includes 1.

location: none
why: The working-age ratio compares the group’s spending with the relevant donor-cell means and significantly exceeds 1, supporting understatement by the transport. The claim appropriately treats the 65+ result as inconclusive.

location: “About 11.1M ... is the right level for early 2025.”
why: A persistent disagreement between surveys does not establish which survey is accurate. The composition evidence and excluded explanations do not independently validate the ACS level, and using an annual 2024 estimate for early 2025 also requires accounting for population change.

location: Treating the CPS–ACS discrepancy as an identified CPS undercount and a correction to early 2025.
why: The evidence establishes a persistent discrepancy and rules out some explanations, but does not establish that the ACS level is correct. A comparison with the 2024 ACS also does not independently identify the true population in early 2025.

location: The 2009 baseline of 117,800 from Prisoners in 2010, compared with a 2021 figure produced by the revised method
why: The 117,800 figure uses the old method that BJS replaced. On the revised basis used from Prisoners in 2011 onward, the 2009 count is 159,800, so the change to 160,100 is +0.2%, essentially flat. The 36% rise is an artifact of the method change, so the contrast of Hispanic growth against other groups' decline fails, and the white figure needs the same same-basis check.

location: The 2009-to-2021 comparison, which puts a figure from the 2011 report (survey-ratio method) next to one from the 2022 report (administrative-record method).
why: The method change alone moved the 31 Dec 2018 count from 168,900 to 121,500, a 28% drop, which is larger than the whole claimed 26% decline. On the new method the count fell only about 2.6% from 2018 to 2021, and on the old method it rose from 2009 to 2018. The white figure crosses the same break, so "fell faster than other groups" is an artefact of the method change.

location: The parser loop `series[col.header] = col.values`, whose output is then used as total encounters.
why: All three blocks have the same headers, so each block overwrites the one before it and only the Field Operations (ports of entry) series survives. That series records programme participants and appointment holders arriving at ports, so the +787% mostly counts the legal pathway itself. Testing whether illegal crossings rose needs the Border Patrol (between ports) series.

location: Parser, `series[col.header] = col.values` inside the loop over the three blocks
why: All three blocks use the same headers, so each block overwrites the one before it. The DataFrame therefore holds only the last block, Border Patrol encounters between ports, not Total. The programme moved these nationalities to ports of entry, where Field Operations encounters rose from about 3,000 to 25,000 a month. The -91% therefore records a shift from crossings between ports to presentations at ports, not a fall in total encounters or workload.

location: Claim: "This is the with-against-without effect", measured by assigning at-fault crashes to the group
why: Charging the group for all damage to other residents in crashes its drivers cause is a fault-based accounting, not a counterfactual. The account's own elasticities (about +0.07 for non-fatal crashes, −0.21 for fatal ones) say that removing the group's vehicle-miles would barely change other residents' crash risk per mile. That puts the with-against-without effect near zero, far below $42.3bn. The comparison to crime fails because other crashes would largely replace the removed ones.

location: Equating the "with-against-without effect" with damage in crashes where group drivers are at fault, net of their liability insurance.
why: Fault attribution is a liability rule; it does not measure what would happen without the group's driving. The account's own elasticity of +1.4, on the networks carrying 65% of the group's driving, means the group's vehicles raise the crash rate for all other drivers, including in crashes where group drivers are not at fault or not involved, and liability insurance does not cover that. Removing about a tenth of urban traffic would cut other residents' crash costs by far more than $9.6bn, so the figure likely understates the effect several times over.

location: The panel filter in acs_cells.py (`imputed_unauthorized == 1` with no Mexican-origin condition)
why: The panel includes imputed-unauthorized noncitizens from every birthplace, and Mexico-born workers earn only about half of those wages. The $6.43bn (and the $4.53bn of payroll tax) is therefore about twice what can be attributed to the Mexican-origin group, roughly $3.2bn and $2.3bn.

location: The `acs_cells.py` panel filter, which has no Mexican-origin condition; its $6.1bn is then credited to the group.
why: imputed_unauthorized` covers noncitizens of every birthplace, so $6.1bn is the withholding of all unauthorized workers. Mexico-born workers earn about half of those wages, so the group's share is roughly $3bn, and crediting the full $6.1bn about doubles it.

location: Adding the aggravated-assault and robbery unit costs, which include a risk-of-homicide component, to the murder costs
why: Assaults and robberies that end in death are recorded as murders, so those deaths are already in the $924. They are counted again through the homicide component: 76% of $380 plus 42% of $60 ≈ $314. With that removed, the gap is about $1,107 and murder's share is about 83%, not 65%.

location: Benefit per worker-year, where the $890 Medicaid savings from avoided nursing-home admissions is added to the $1,420 value of care hours
why: The source note says 61% of the $21.70 unit value is already the avoided cost of institutional care. 61% of $1,420 is about $866, almost exactly the $890 Medicaid line, so the same avoided nursing-home cost is counted twice. The evidence supports about $1,420, and $2,310 overstates it by roughly 60%.

location: The premise that a low spending response "cannot coexist with no dilution", and the calculation that multiplies all uncharged spending by the 0.61 instructional share.
why: Fixed costs and spare capacity make an extra pupil cost less than the average pupil, which by itself produces an enrollment elasticity below 1 with no dilution. Those fixed costs are mostly non-instructional, so applying the 0.61 share overstates the harm. The $16.1bn assumes no economies of scale and uses only the first-years response. The long-run response gives $3.6bn, the direct class-size pathway gives $2.6bn, and the range crosses zero, so neither "most" nor the central figure is supported.

location: The calculation step "no shortfall in spending per pupil, so no forgone instructional spending per incumbent pupil".
why: Keeping average spending per pupil constant does not keep incumbents' spending constant when the added pupils draw above-average resources. 31% of the group's pupils carry English-learner weights of 20-25%, which is about 6-8% above average per pupil. With an elasticity of about 1.0, that premium either comes out of incumbents' spending or is missed by the average-cost charge, and the two-year lag adds some temporary dilution as well.

location: The 2000 data point (0.13), because of how the 2000 census imputed birthplace for institutionalized men (QBPL flag)
why: In 2000, 68% of institutionalized Mexican-origin men had an imputed birthplace, and 98% of those were assigned a US birth, while 38.5% of the men who reported a birthplace were foreign-born. If the imputed men resemble the reporters, the census counts only about 0.32×0.385 + 0.68×0.02 ≈ 0.14 of the group as foreign-born against a true 0.385, an undercount of about 2.8×, which moves the 0.13 ratio to about 0.37. The 1980–1990 change (0.45 to 0.42) is within its SEs, and the censuses handle missing birthplace differently, so no cohort-by-cohort improvement is shown.

location: Round 3 birthplace imputation, and different handling of missing birthplaces across rounds
why: Round 3 imputes birthplace for 64% of institutionalized Mexican-origin men and marks 91% of those as foreign-born. Among men who reported a birthplace, only 38.5% were foreign-born. Because the donors were household residents, the imputation roughly doubles the foreign-born count (72% vs 38.5%; the ratio falls to about 0.6 if imputed cases matched reporters), while rounds 1–2 simply dropped missing birthplaces. The jump to 1.10 is therefore mostly a data-processing artifact, and the step from 0.45 to 0.48 is within noise (SE of the difference ≈0.07).

location: The step from equal skip rates (18.1% vs 18.2%) to "no bias", given that the income hot deck does not match on Hispanic origin
why: Hot-deck bias depends on who the donors are, not on how often people skip. Without Hispanic origin in the match, the group's nonrespondents mostly get donors from outside the group. As a result, the fill-ins keep only 9% of the group's wage gap (DiD +0.139, about 3 SE) and raise Social Security, pension and interest income by 19–66 log points. Running those incomes through a tax calculator overstates the group's taxable income and tax.

location: "skip the income supplement at the same rate … so … fill-ins included"
why: Equal skip rates do not prevent bias when donor cells are not matched on Hispanic origin or citizenship. The group's respondents report SSI and public assistance at 0.58 times the rate of others, but its filled-in records show 0.97 times, and the filled-in amounts are 37–41 log points higher. The fill-ins therefore inflate the group's receipt, and keys that allocate national totals by these CPS amounts give the group too large a share.

location: The step from "returnees have less schooling than never-migrants" to "the US stayers' average schooling rises"
why: Whether return migration raises the stayers' average depends on how returnees compare with the emigrants who stay in the US, not with people who never left Mexico. Mexican emigrants as a group already have less schooling than non-migrants, so returnees at 7.9 years could be above the stayers' mean. The survey does not observe the stayers, as its stated limitation says.

location: The inference from the returnee-versus-non-migrant gap (+1.2 years) to "US stayers' average schooling falls"
why: Return migration lowers the US stayers' average only if returnees have more schooling than the migrants who remain in the US. Comparing them with people who never left Mexico cannot show that, and the limitation says the survey does not observe emigrants still in the US. If stayers average more than 10.8 years, return migration raises their mean.

location: The claim that the 24,000 count "is an upper bound", and the claim that noncitizen voting is orders of magnitude too small, set against margins of 6 and 187 votes
why: The audits leave out many states and cannot flag anyone never recorded as a noncitizen, so the true number could be higher. False positives push the other way, so the net direction is unknown and 24,000 is not an upper bound. Even taken at face value, 24,000 votes spread across 435 House districts averages about 55 per district, which is more than Iowa-2's 6-vote margin and within one order of magnitude of CA-13's 187, so ruling out any decided contest would need district-level counts.

location: "about 24,000 noncitizen ballots … a lower bound", and the step from that figure to CA-13
why: The 24,000 are record-match flags, many later cleared as naturalized citizens, and none are confirmed as ballots cast by noncitizens. That makes the figure at most an upper bound on flags, not a lower bound on ballots. California published no audit, so no evidence puts any flagged ballot in CA-13, let alone a net of more than 187 for the winner.

location: founder_profile`. The status adjustment applies only at ages 18–64. At 65+ the pooled profile applies whatever the status.
why: The model gives an unauthorized founder and a legalized founder the same senior profile. Legalization therefore cannot change Social Security, Medicare or Medicaid eligibility, which is where status matters most, and seniors carry 34.4% of the gap. The 1.9% result comes from how the model is built, not from the data.

location: founder_profile`: only `p.benefits` changes on legalization, and earnings and taxes stay on `unauthorized_profile`
why: Legalization switches on eligibility for Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid and SSI, but earnings and taxes stay at the unauthorized level. The cited studies show wage gains of 6–15% and a large shift of work onto payroll records. The model counts the extra costs of legal status but leaves out the extra revenue, so the 34% rise is biased upward and could be much smaller.

location: The outcome variable, which is the SSI receipt rate across all households because the 2000 file has no nativity split.
why: Immigrant households receive SSI at 1.9% and native households at 4.6%, so a 1-point shift toward immigrant households lowers the all-household rate by about 0.027pp even if natives' receipt does not change. That accounts for nearly all of the −0.03 estimate. The implied effect on natives is about zero, with an interval reaching roughly +0.02pp. Arrivals after 1996 were largely ineligible for SSI, so the composition effect could exceed 0.03pp and hide some displacement. The estimate is not better evidence against displacement.

location: The outcome, which is receipt across all households with no nativity split, combined with the group-specific rates (6.9% for immigrant households, 4.2% for native ones)
why: Composition alone predicts this result. A 1-point rise in immigrant share raises the all-household rate by 0.01 × (6.9 − 4.2) = 0.027 pp, which is nearly the whole 0.03 estimate. The implied effect on natives is about 0.003 pp (SE 0.012), so the data give no evidence that natives are pushed onto transfer programmes.

location: none
why: The claims are limited to within-state changes, and the evidence states that level effects and national shifts are not identified. The weakness of the English-learner estimate is disclosed, and the cohort-aligned version is larger (−0.070) and robust. The $1bn roughly checks out: 0.035 × 0.18 ≈ 0.0063 SD, times about 10% earnings per SD, times about $1M present-value earnings, times about 1.9M white pupils per cohort ≈ $1bn. Using −0.070 instead would roughly double it.

location: none
why: Each named threat gets a check: NAEP's absolute scale, cut scores and exit-exam repeal unrelated to the shares, region-by-year effects, state trends, and the cohort design with no lead. The limits are stated. The $11bn is explicitly conditional and the arithmetic holds (≈0.07 SD × ~1.8–2M pupils × ~10–13% earnings per SD × ~$0.6–0.8M present value of lifetime earnings). White families leaving public schools, which are the only schools state NAEP samples, is an untested risk, but it does not overturn the hedged claim.

location: none

Moving tax toward bins where the group's share is higher raises its tax, and 321.8 − 3.2 = 318.6. The held-out year, the 2022 baseline (2.4pp) and the $500k pooling check (+$3.1bn, SE 0.5) support the finding, and it is presented as a candidate that was not adopted.

location: none
why: The numbers are consistent. With a total variation of 8.4pp and all of the excess at $50k–$200k, the shortfalls must also sum to 8.4pp: 3.3pp at $200k–$1M and the remaining 5.1pp elsewhere, mostly in the pooled $1M+ bin. Moving tax from bins where the group is 6–12% of people to bins where it is 4% or less must lower the group's tax, and 321.8 + 3.2 = 325.0. The key scores better on the held-out year than on its own base year, the pooling sensitivity is shown, and the adjustment is not adopted.

location: none

California's supplement is concentrated where the group lives, so the +0.96 comes from comparing against the wrong definition. The federal-only comparison is the one definition that matches the account's line, not a favourable choice among several, and it is labelled as post hoc. Given how little power state totals have (the refundable-credit interval runs from about -$5bn to +$8bn), +0.17 does not justify a correction.

location: none
why: The target was switched after seeing the data, but the claim says so, and the switch fixes a real mismatch. The account's SSI line includes the California-heavy state supplements while the first target covers federal payments only, so a group concentrated in California would get a negative delta, which matches the -0.48. On the matching target, -0.08 is small given how little power state totals have; calling the decisive comparison "blind" overstates it but does not change the conclusion.

location: none
why: The pre-committed test shows what the claim says: keys based on the uninsured fit state shares much better than a population key (0.134, and 0.126 for a plain count, against 0.210). The caveats are disclosed and handled. The person-year refinement adds nothing, the group-specific slope is confounded by region controls added after the data were seen and is not adopted, and insured patients' amounts in line 30 mostly tilt the benchmark toward the population key, which makes the test conservative. Because line 30 includes insured patients, the 0.88 ratio overstates agreement on the national total, but the claim draws no conclusion about that total.

location: none
why: The predictions and scoring rule were committed before the reports were opened. The direction is right: the group's share of the uninsured is well above its population share, so a population key lowers its charge. The claim stops at "candidate, not adopted." The disclosed limits (line 30 includes insured patients' uncompensated care, the region controls were added after seeing the data, and the national totals differ at a ratio of 0.88) weaken the case for switching but fit that hedged wording.

location: none
why: Booking, in the exposure year, the present value of the lifetime loss that year causes is standard incidence-based accrual, like a pension's normal cost. Each year's exposure is counted once, 13 years of harm is 13 one-year accruals, and the tax loss appears only inside the social loss. The stated conditions are the ones that prevent a stock/flow error or double counting. This holds if each year's effect is estimated as the effect of one extra year, which the evidence implies.

location: none
why: Each year's exposure adds a new increment to human capital, so that increment is a flow for the year. Booking its present value once works the same way as a pension-service accrual, and 13 years of exposure give 13 increments, not 13 lifetimes. The tax gain is already inside the gross earnings gain, so leaving it out of the fiscal line prevents counting it twice.

location: none
why: The victim unit costs leave out police, courts and corrections, which enter only through the justice budget lines, so the two lines do not overlap. Deaths are counted once because the homicide-risk component is removed from assault and robbery and homicides have their own row. The only leftover risk is small: another crime type, such as rape, might still carry a homicide-risk component.

location: none
why: The price line counts only other residents' consumer savings. It leaves out the group's own consumption and firms' profits, whose taxes sit in receipts, and wage effects are booked separately. No dollar appears in both the price line and the receipts line. Counting other residents' wage losses and their price gains separately is the standard split of transfers and surplus, not double counting.

location: none
why: Every reported variant leaves winners in the minority: 18.7–29.2% across elasticities, 10.3% with halved wage dispersion and at most 30.5% across the channel choices. The claim is stated as conditional on allocation. The numbers are internally consistent, since a higher elasticity or halved dispersion shrinks wage deviations and cuts winners at about the rate the scaling predicts. The only untested direction is more wage dispersion, which the conditional wording covers.

location: none
